title: child protection and vulnerable families: trends and issues in the australian context
display_name: Child Protection and Vulnerable Families: Trends and Issues in the Australian Context
abstract: this paper will provide an overview and analysis of developments in child protection and out of home care in australia. it will outline early responses to perceived inadequate parenting to provide the historical and policy contexts of contemporary debates on, and responses to, the care and protection of children and young people. child maltreatment affects a large number of children across australia. the statistics of reported maltreatment reflect striking increases over time. over the last decade, several public inquiries into the operation of child protection have been undertaken in a number of state jurisdictions following which some states have embarked on large scale reform of legislation and policy, to either strengthen the child protection mandate, or refocus services. some exemplars of significant reform in selected states will be cited. some of the themes that will be explored in the paper will include the impact of major state based public inquiries, overseas reviews and research on child protection policy and practice; the changing balance between orientations to child protection and family support, the parameters of out of home care, the high levels of governmental intervention experienced by aboriginal and torres strait islander families, and a critical appraisal of major transformations in protective care.

title: refugee integration policy: the effects of uk policy-making on refugees in scotland
display_name: Refugee Integration Policy: The Effects of UK Policy-Making on Refugees in Scotland
abstract: abstract while the concept of migrant integration is a contested one, national, sub-national and local governments over the past forty to fifty years have professed support for integration in various forms. however, practical measures have been rare, with broad race-relations policies from the 1960s being the primary means of inclusion . under new labour, refugees were identified as a migrant population with particular challenges and they have been the only migrant group subject to specific integration programmes. nevertheless, policy and rhetoric about asylum seekers and refugees more generally have tended to operate against integration and have made it increasingly difficult for refugees to rebuild their lives. this paper examines refugee integration from the perspectives of the refugees themselves, using both qualitative and quantitative methods. it also looks at the governance of integration in scotland and highlights scottish distinctiveness vis- -vis the uk. the article suggests that the consequences of broader uk government policy around asylum and refugee issues negates any positive support in the form of refugee integration programmes and actively inhibits integration.

abstract: abstract astrocytes are a target for regenerative neurobiology because in brain injury their phenotype arbitrates brain integrity, neuronal death and subsequent repair and reconstruction. we explored the ability of 3d scaffolds to direct astrocytes into phenotypes with the potential to support neuronal survival. poly caprolactone scaffolds were electrospun with random and aligned fibre orientations on which murine astrocytes were sub cultured and analysed at 4 and 12 div. astrocytes survived, proliferated and migrated into scaffolds adopting 3d morphologies, mimicking in vivo stellated phenotypes. cells on random poly caprolactone scaffolds grew as circular colonies extending processes deep within sub micron fibres, whereas astrocytes on aligned scaffolds exhibited rectangular colonies with processes following not only the direction of fibre alignment but also penetrating the scaffold. cell viability was maintained over 12 div, and cytochemistry for f /g actin showed fewer stress fibres on bioscaffolds relative to 2d astrocytes. reduced cytoskeletal stress was confirmed by the decreased expression of glial fibrillary acidic protein. pcr demonstrated up regulation of genes (excitatory amino acid transporter 2, brain derived neurotrophic factor and anti oxidant) reflecting healthy biologies of mature astrocytes in our extended culture protocol. this study illustrates the therapeutic potential of bioengineering strategies using 3d electrospun scaffolds which direct astrocytes into phenotypes supporting brain repair. image astrocytes exist in phenotypes with pro survival and destructive components, and their biology can be modulated by changing phenotype. our findings demonstrate murine astrocytes adopt a healthy phenotype when cultured in 3d. astrocytes proliferate and extend into poly caprolactone scaffolds displaying 3d stellated morphologies with reduced gfap expression and actin stress fibres, plus a cytotrophic gene profile. bioengineered 3d scaffolds have potential to direct inflammation to aid regenerative neurobiology.

inredditemailqr code sectionsmorein 1928, afro-martiniquean literary salonist jane nardal published her groundbreaking essay internationalism noir (black internationalism) in la d p che africaine a black anticolonial magazine cofounded and edited by her sister paulette nardal. forecasting the negritude movement of the 1930s, the paris-based jane nardal argued that the new negro movement would inspire the global emergence of a generation of afro-latin and francophone artists and writers whose work would be collectively centered on the historical study of the black race.1over time, black activists, scholars, and intellectuals would use black internationalism in far more expansive ways: as an insurgent political culture emerging in response to slavery, colonialism, and white imperialism; to describe the political and cultural ways black communities raised global questions of struggle; to underscore the african diaspora s self-engagement beyond the boundaries of european colonial and nation-states; and to capture the black world s relationships with the global south. even before the term gained common parlance among academics, numerous writers merze tate, w.e.b. du bois, and kwame nkrumah among them employed black internationalism as an idea viewed through the lenses of pan-africanism, communism, garveyism, socialism, and black power.nearly one hundred years since nardal s crucial essay, black internationalism has grown from a visionary phrase into a vibrant subfield of africana studies and related disciplines one that is bursting with debate, promise, and new revelations.2 the past few decades alone have witnessed a striking growth of studies framed under the banner of black internationalism best described as a global political, intellectual, and artistic movement of african descended people engaged in a collective struggle to overthrow global white supremacy in its many forms. 3 moving beyond a nation-state-centered level of analysis, these studies have significantly expanded our conception of black internationalism revealing the various ways people of african descent articulated global visions of freedom and worked to forge transnational solidarities with people of color across the world. despite the growth of the field, there remains much work to be done to expand the contours of black internationalism theoretically, spatially, and temporally. this special issue features groundbreaking scholarship in the field from a diverse range of scholars across subfields. its sampling of innovative contributions, approaches, methods, and methodologies helps deepen our understanding of how black internationalism shaped us and global history.the first two essays in the issue an organic union by christina cecelia davidson and virginia in the pacific by guy emerson mount examine black internationalism during the late nineteenth and early twentieth centuries. through a close reading of the african methodist episcopal (ame) church s archival documents, davidson examines black protest and resistance against the idea of ecclesiastical imperialism during the late nineteenth century. in 1880, african american religious leaders gathered for a pivotal ame conference in st. louis, missouri, where they engaged in spirited debate about the future of the denomination. as many considered the feasibility of a merger with the british methodist episcopal church, others vehemently opposed the idea. the voices raised in opposition that came to dominate the discussion accentuate the deep significance of religion and spirituality within the black internationalist discourses of the period. the conference brought to the fore the crucial question of how black people in the united states should respond to us empire and white supremacy. davidson s article unveils how black religious leaders in the ame grappled with ideas of pan-africanism and worked to resist the expansion of white supremacist projections within the realm of religion.mount s virginia in the pacific shifts the focus to the realm of education. he draws on an array of previously underutilized archival sources to chart the life and work of early twentieth-century black educator helen james. born in 1876, james grew up in hartford, connecticut, and went on to attend hampton university before becoming a teacher at hawai i s kona orphanage. by examining her career, mount challenges scholars of black internationalism to consider the intermingling of us imperial ambitions in the atlantic and the pacific. he highlights the connections between the origins of industrial education in american outposts in the pacific and how those ideas then influenced the founding of institutions such as hampton after the american civil war. after graduating from these newly founded schools, students like james traveled abroad and returned this form of education to the united states pacific colonies. mount traces the complicated transnational lineage of industrial education to reveal the contours of the american imperial project and to further explore the development of the black pacific. 4in producing a black world, celeste day moore considers black internationalism s routes from the united states to the african continent. here she sheds new light on how internationalist ideas permeated black media and film through an exploration of the life and influence of filmmaker william greaves, the executive producer of the national educational television program black journal. as part of public television s response to the 1968 kerner commission and the assassination of martin luther king jr., black journal offered informed commentary on the black freedom struggle in the united states and its connection to contemporary liberation movements in ethiopia, south africa, nigeria, and other parts of africa. a worldwide traveler during the 1950s, greaves had expanded his skills as a filmmaker and built a strong network of pan-africanist friends and associates. under his editorial leadership, black journal adopted a black internationalist perspective in its programming, which innovatively included the use of african languages such as swahili and yoruba. while the show highlighted key developments taking place in the united states, moore argues that it was never constrained by the nation-state. to the contrary, black journal was committed to covering african liberation movements, including the antiapartheid struggle in south africa. moore s exploration of william greaves influence on black journal s programming demonstrates how internationalist ideas shaped black media, film, and culture.tiana wilson s article, spain s queen of soul, offers another compelling example of how internationalism shaped black culture during the twentieth century. building on the scholarship of keisha n. blain, tiffany gill, bianca c. williams, and others, wilson examines expressions of black internationalism that move beyond the framework of political struggle and instead reveal the varied ways black women engaged in internationalist activism through leisure, religious practices, performance, and artistic expression.5 providing insight into the life of jazz expatriate donna hightower, wilson highlights the disparate paths and strategies of black women s transnational and transracial partnerships during the twentieth century. wilson s trendsetting examination of hightower one of the first scholarly, full-life treatments of the performer tracks her participation in political activism, public-self fashioning, and black religious internationalism from the late 1960s to the 1980s. hightower s journey as an expatriate in spain started with the singer s recognition that her career could not advance in the united states against its backdrop of racism, discrimination, and violence. through the spanish press, hightower denounced systemic racism in the united states and pointed out the ways it harmed and stifled black communities. she also challenged the depictions of black womanhood and motherhood by sharing aspects of her private life, including details about her marriage and divorce. these disclosures and her turn toward a gospel music tradition that celebrated black protestantism reveal how hightower compelled a predominantly white audience in spain to reckon with blackness and their own ideas about race, religion, gender, and sexuality.drawing on a rich archive of university records, historical newspapers, and oral histories, bright gyamfi s from nkrumah s black star to the african diaspora also highlights the significance of travel and migration as vehicles for advancing black internationalist movements and discourses. while much of the extant literature has focused on the activist work of black americans abroad, gyamfi s original essay centers on the historical contributions of african intellectuals in the united states. here, he examines the activism and intellectual pursuits of three ghanaian scholars in the united states during the 1970s and 1980s: nana kobina nketsia iv, dovi afesi, and anani dzidzienyo. these three scholars played transformative and long-lasting roles in shaping black studies, advocating for the discipline s programs and black intellectuals more broadly to incorporate a diasporic understanding of africa into their curricula. they also established archives at these programs to drive further research among students and others in the area of africana studies. gyamfi s essay adds the ideas and experiences of nketsia, afesi, and dzidienyo to those of the black student activists who demanded the formation of black studies programs at universities throughout the united states. against the backdrop of the black power era, these three scholars challenged the stigmatized view of africa held by many americans and encouraged african american intellectuals to expand their engagement with africa beyond the lens of the transatlantic slave trade and focus on contemporary developments on the continent.in the final essay, benjamin d. weber ties the history of human rights activism to the imprisoned black radical tradition by unpacking the creative strategies that black intellectuals and activists used to rebel against the carceral state. weber argues that this strategy coalesced into an anticarceral internationalism, as imprisoned individuals connected their plights to the global struggle against racism, sexism, and colonization. the internationalist framing of these campaigns most recently deployed after the murders of george floyd and breonna taylor has expanded human rights discourse to consider concrete demands as opposed to the platitudes often offered by state actors. the theory of human rights emerging from anticarceral activism includes amending the right to life to include a right to breathe free from the fear of state violence and a carceral state designed to uphold the racial order; the right to resist against exploitation through defense committees and self-defense; the right to repair and demand restitution for past human rights abuses; and a right to reenvision societal structures through abolition. weber s research helps to illuminate intellectuals and activists often marginalized in mainstream narratives and demonstrates the expansive international visions within the imprisoned black radical tradition.while this special issue does not purport to comprehensively address all the critical questions of black internationalism, its six essays help us to reconceptualize both the history and contemporary relevance of black internationalism. they highlight its varied articulations since the late nineteenth century and even grapple with its limitations. by shedding light on expressions of black internationalism in diverse spaces, these works reflect the field s remarkable growth in the areas of culture, geography, and methodology. perhaps more critically, the essays in this special issue powerfully reveal the links between past and present. the questions that they raise about black internationalism s intersections with religion, culture, music, gender, the carceral state, archives, education, black travel, and media are as just as relevant today as they have ever been.close to a hundred years since jane nardal s pivotal appeal, black internationalism continues to shape contemporary social movements, political philosophies, and strategies in every part of the globe in which black people find themselves the americas, africa, europe, asia and oceania. the most visible sign of this phenomenon is arguably the global reach of the black lives matter movement. still, the contours of black internationalism have led us to other queries as well, including race and political economy, indigeneity, visual art, poetics, immigration, sports activism, reparations, afrofuturism, identity, and radical imagination. the impulse among people of african descent to look beyond the nation-state to forge transnational collaborations and solidarities with other marginalized groups remains a powerful response to racism and white supremacy. under the banner of black internationalism, black people in the african diaspora remain vigilant in the effort to dismantle systems of oppression, challenge stereotypical images of black people in the media and other venues, and disrupt racial hierarchies that reinforce discrimination and inequality. these overlapping efforts offer a beacon of hope in these turbulent times.noteskeisha n. blain is associate professor of title: what has economics to say about racial discrimination?
display_name: What Has Economics to Say About Racial Discrimination?
abstract: racial discrimination pervades every aspect of a society in which it is found. it is found above all in attitudes of both races, but also in social relations, in intermarriage, in residential location, and, frequently, in legal barriers. it is also found in levels of economic accomplishment; that is, income, wages, prices paid, and credit extended. it is natural to suppose that economic analysis can cast light on the economic effects of racial discrimination. but the pervasiveness of the phenomenon must give us pause. can a phenomenon manifest everywhere in the social world really be understood, even in only one aspect, by the tools of a single discipline? i want to explore here the scope and limits of ordinary economic analysis for understanding racial discrimination even in markets.

title: civic and ethno belonging among recent refugees to australia
display_name: Civic and Ethno Belonging among Recent Refugees to Australia
abstract: australia offers some of the best government-funded settlement services in the world to refugees who come through its official resettlement programme. these services cater to their material, medical and, to some extent, their social needs. however, services cannot provide a sense of belonging to people uprooted from their homelands and transplanted to a culturally and geographically distant place. or can they? this article explores the facets of belonging identified inductively from a corpus of data from qualitative interviews with 77 refugees living in western australia. thematically, these map clearly onto civic and ethno conceptualizations of the nation-state and belonging within it. while refugees assert their civic belonging in terms of access to services and rights available to refugees and to australians more broadly, their sense of ethno belonging is much more ambivalent, due to experiences with the mainstream population. implications in regard to the concept of the nation-state, and for processes of integration and social inclusion, are considered.
